title: What localhost is and how to see your project running
promise: You're going to have your project open in the browser. You'll know how to start and stop it on your own whenever you want. And when the screen goes blank, you'll be able to tell in under a minute which of the three blanks it is. You'll also know what to do about each one.
why: Nacho runs a bike shop in Zaragoza and wanted a website with his catalog. He asked Claude for help, Claude set up the files and told him "now run npm run dev and open localhost:3000." Nacho did it, the browser told him it couldn't reach the site, and he assumed the website was broken. He spent two days asking the AI to fix code that had absolutely nothing wrong with it. The server had started on port 3001 because 3000 was taken by something else. And that number was written right on his screen from the start. Nobody had taught him how to read it.

theory.title: Localhost is your own computer acting as the waiter
theory.text: When you type amazon.com, your browser sends a request out through your router. That request travels to a data center hundreds of miles away. There, a running computer sends the page back. Localhost is exactly the same thing, with one difference: the computer sending the page back is yours, the one in front of you. The word localhost literally means "this machine." Its number equivalent is 127.0.0.1, an address reserved worldwide to mean "right here." The request doesn't go out through the router, doesn't touch the internet, and your ISP never sees it. It turns around inside your computer and comes back. The doubt that'll come up is whether that means your website is already published. The answer is no, not even close. If you send the link localhost:3000 to your business partner over WhatsApp, he won't see your website. He'll see an error, or, if he happens to have another project running, he'll see his own. On his computer, localhost means his computer. And that, which sounds like a limitation, is the best news in the lesson. You can break whatever you want, delete half the page, type nonsense, and experiment. Not a single human being on the planet is watching. On top of that it costs nothing: running your project locally is always $0, no card, no account, no time limit.
theory.analogy: Publishing a website is opening a restaurant on the street: anyone can walk in. Localhost is cooking at home: you can burn the omelet four times and nobody knows. Same stove, same pan, same recipe, zero witnesses.
theory.example: Nacho sent his brother the link http://localhost:3000 hoping for feedback on the catalog. His brother replied "I'm getting an error." Neither of them had done anything wrong: on his brother's phone, localhost means his brother's phone.

theory.title: The number after the colon is a door, and you have to read it, not guess it
theory.text: In localhost:3000, the 3000 is the port. Your computer can have several programs listening at once. The port is the number that tells them apart: one answers at door 3000, another at 5173, another at 8000. Without that number the browser wouldn't know which one to ask. Every tool has its customary number, and it's worth them sounding familiar. Next.js and Create React App start on 3000, and Vite on 5173. A Python server starts on 8000, Flask on 5000, and Streamlit on 8501. Here's the failure that trips up the most people, the same one that got Nacho. If the port a tool wants is already taken by another program, the tool doesn't complain. It jumps to the next free one, starts on 3001 or 3002, and writes it on screen. You, meanwhile, keep typing 3000 into the browser because that's what the tutorial said. And you see an error that has nothing to do with you. The rule is short and saves you days. The right address is told to you by the terminal every time you start it: your job is to read it there, not memorize it. Look for the line that says "Local:" or "running on" and copy it as-is.
theory.analogy: An office building's address gets you to the lobby. The port number is the specific buzzer: apartment 4B. Ringing the lobby and expecting the physical therapist from 4B to come down doesn't work no matter how well you know the street.
theory.example: Nacho had the shop's website running in one window and, without remembering, opened another terminal to test a second idea. The second one started on 3001 and the screen said so: "Port 3000 is in use, using 3001 instead." That eleven-word sentence was the solution to his two wasted days.

theory.title: The dev server is a program that has to stay running
theory.text: To see your project, a program needs to be running and answering requests. That program is called the development server. It's usually turned on by typing npm run dev into the terminal. The terminal is the black window where you type commands instead of clicking buttons. When you launch it, something happens that scares everyone the first time. The terminal spits out a few lines and goes still, not giving you the cursor back to type more. That's not it hanging, it's exactly the opposite: it's working, and it'll keep doing so until you stop it. It stops with Ctrl+C, both keys at once, inside that same window. And here's the part you need to internalize. If you close the terminal window, shut down the computer, or the computer sleeps, the website stops existing. It exists again once you start it up again. Your project hasn't been deleted, the files are still there intact; there's just nobody serving the page. Every time you sit down to work, the first move of the day is opening the terminal in the project folder and starting it up. Every time you're done, Ctrl+C and move on.
theory.analogy: It's a TV that's on, not a photo. Turn off the TV and no channel gets erased, but you stop seeing the picture. Press the button again and everything's still there.
theory.example: Nacho closed the terminal on a Thursday at eight in the evening because having it open bothered him. Friday morning he opened the browser and saw the error. He wrote to Claude "my website broke overnight." Nothing had broken: he just needed to press Enter once.

theory.title: Save and see the change instantly: hot reload
theory.text: This is the part that hooks you. With the server running, you change a word in a file and press Ctrl+S to save. Before you finish moving your hand, the browser has already updated on its own. It's called hot reload, and it's not a gimmick. It's what makes working with AI bearable. You ask for a change, it writes it, and you see it with no extra step at all. The way I recommend working from now on is having two windows at once. The browser on the left and the AI on the right. And never closing either during a session. Now the doubt that'll come up: you changed something and nothing happens on screen. There are almost always three reasons, in this order. One, you haven't saved the file, and the editor tab's title is telling you with a dot next to the name. Two, the terminal wrote a red error and the change never even got applied. Three, you touched one of the files that really does require a restart. Those are the config files and the environment variable ones (the .env file, where keys are stored). It also happens when something new gets installed. In that third case, Ctrl+C and starting it again fixes it in five seconds.
theory.example: Nacho changed the title from "Nacho's Shop" to "Nacho's Bikes — Zaragoza" and pressed Ctrl+S. The browser tab's name changed before he'd even let go of the keys. Four tenths of a second. That was the first time in his life it felt like his.

theory.title: A blank screen isn't one thing, it's three, and they don't get fixed the same way
theory.text: This is where people give up, and they give up by confusing three situations that look the same and have nothing to do with each other. Blank A is when the browser writes its own message. For example: "This site can't be reached," "localhost refused to connect," or ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED. Notice that text is written by the browser, not your project. It means the page never came into existence. The server isn't running, or it crashed, or you're calling the wrong port. This is 80% of cases and gets fixed by looking at the terminal, not the code. Blank B is a truly white blank screen, completely empty, with no message, but with the project's title in the tab up top. That means the page did arrive and broke while rendering, almost always due to a code error. The explanation is waiting for you in the browser console. Blank C is a screen with a big error message, sometimes on a red background, with file names and line numbers. That's not a problem, it's a gift: it's telling you exactly where to point your finger. And before touching absolutely anything in all three cases: check the terminal. If there's red text there, it's already told you what's happening and you'll save half the work.
theory.analogy: Blank A is ringing a doorbell and nobody's home. Blank B is walking in and finding the house dark. Blank C is walking in and finding a note stuck to the fridge that says "the power's out, the breaker's in the hallway." Looking for the breaker when the real problem is nobody's home gets you nowhere.
theory.example: Nacho's two lost days were a pure blank A: "localhost refused the connection." He treated it like a blank B and spent forty messages asking the AI to review the catalog's code. The code was perfect from minute one.

theory.title: The browser console: where the missing answer is written
theory.text: Inside any browser there's a hidden screen where the page keeps a log of everything that happens to it, errors included. It opens with the F12 key, or with Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows and Cmd+Option+J on Mac, and closes the same way. A side panel opens with tabs, and the two that matter to you are "Console" and "Network." In the console you'll see colored lines, and the red ones are the errors. Now the real doubt, the one that stops people: you're not going to understand what it says, and you don't need to. Your job isn't to interpret it: it's to copy it and paste it to the AI exactly as-is. The same way you'd show an X-ray to a doctor. Two details that make you look like a pro. Copy the first red error, not the last, because the first usually triggers all the others in a cascade. And ignore the yellow warnings, which show up on every website in the world and almost never mean anything. In the "Network" tab, if you see red lines with a 404 next to them, it means the page was requesting a file that doesn't exist. Usually an image or a misnamed stylesheet.
theory.example: The error that wins the prize in new projects is "Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')". Sounds like gibberish and means one very silly thing: the website was trying to render a product list that was still empty. Nacho pasted that line into Claude without changing a comma and had it fixed in the second message.

tasks.title: Ask the AI for your project's startup sheet
tasks.where: In the Claude, ChatGPT, or Gemini app, in the conversation where you're building your project
tasks.action: Open the conversation where the AI created your project (if you have several, the most recent one) and paste the prompt below. What you want isn't a nice explanation, but four specific facts you'll use every day. Which folder to be in, what to type to start it, what exact address to open, and how to stop it. When it answers, don't close that response: you'll need it in the next task.
tasks.prompt:
I'm working on the project we built in this conversation. I don't know how to code and the terminal intimidates me, so I need literal instructions, no implied steps.

Give me a startup sheet with exactly these five points, each on its own line, no intro paragraphs:

1. The full path of the folder I need to be in before typing anything.
2. The exact command that opens the terminal already positioned in that folder, for my operating system (tell me which you're assuming: Windows, Mac, or Linux).
3. The exact command that starts the project, written to copy and paste as-is.
4. The full address I need to type into the browser, with http:// in front and the port number included, and warn me whether that number can change and where I read it if it does.
5. How to stop the server when I'm done.

After the sheet, tell me in two sentences what the terminal looks like when it started CORRECTLY: what specific line I should see to know it worked. And warn me whether the terminal is going to stay without giving me the cursor back, so I don't think it hung.

If the project needs any preliminary step done only the first time (installing dependencies, creating a config file), put that before everything and mark it "first time only."
tasks.expect: A five-line list with a real folder path (something like C:\Users\yourname\projects\bikes). Plus a startup command (almost always npm run dev) and an address with the port included (http://localhost:3000). No filler paragraphs.
tasks.stuck: If it answers with a generic internet tutorial instead of looking at YOUR project, reply: "Don't give me general instructions. Look at this project's files, specifically package.json, and tell me what command is actually written there." If it doesn't have access to your files because you're working just by chat, paste the contents of the package.json file and repeat the question.

tasks.title: Start the server and read the address on screen
tasks.where: In your computer's terminal, positioned in the project folder
tasks.action: Open the terminal the way the AI told you in the previous task. On Windows the easiest way is to open the project folder in File Explorer. Click the address bar up top, clear what's there, type powershell, and press Enter. A blue window opens already positioned in that folder. On Mac, right-click the folder, then "Services," then "New Terminal at Folder." Type the startup command, press Enter, and wait five to thirty seconds without touching anything. When it stops printing things, look for a line that says "Local:" followed by an address, or "running on," or "ready." That address is the right one. Write down the port number on paper.
tasks.expect: Several lines of text and, among them, something like "Local: http://localhost:3000". The cursor doesn't come back, the window just sits there with a little cursor blinking. That's correct: it means it's running and waiting.
tasks.stuck: If "npm is not recognized as a command" shows up, Node.js needs installing. That's done from nodejs.org, downloading the LTS version. Tell the AI to walk you through it and come back to this task after. If "Missing script: dev" shows up, your project's startup command is different. Type npm run by itself and press Enter, and it'll list the ones that do exist. If a wall of red text shows up, copy it in full, paste it to the AI, and add: "This shows up when starting. Tell me in one sentence what's missing and the exact command to fix it."

tasks.title: Open your project in the browser and bookmark it
tasks.where: In your browser, with the previous task's terminal still open
tasks.action: Without closing the terminal, open Chrome, Edge, or whichever browser you use. Click the address bar up top and clear it. Type the exact address you read in the terminal, with http:// and the port number: for example http://localhost:3000. Press Enter. Once you see it, press Ctrl+D (Cmd+D on Mac) to bookmark it and give it a recognizable name, like "MY WEBSITE — local." That way tomorrow you don't have to remember the number.
tasks.expect: Your project on screen. It can be ugly, half-finished, full of placeholder text: doesn't matter, that's the moment. And in the terminal you'll see new lines show up every time you reload, since it's logging every visit.
tasks.stuck: If the browser takes you to a search engine instead of your website, you typed the address without http://. It got treated as a search: type it in full again. If it says it can't reach the site, go to the terminal and check two things. That it's still open and running, and that the number you typed matches what's shown there. Nine times out of ten, that's it.

tasks.title: Change one word and check hot reload
tasks.where: In the AI app, with the browser and terminal open side by side
tasks.action: Put the browser window on the left half of the screen and the AI on the right. On Windows, drag each window against the side edge and it snaps into place. Paste the prompt below, swapping the bracketed text for something visible on your website. Once the AI saves the change, don't touch the browser: watch it update on its own.
tasks.prompt:
I want to check my project's auto-reload works before I get into building anything serious.

Change the text "[write the text currently shown on your website here]" to "[write the new text you want to see here]". It's a one-line change: don't touch any other file, don't reorganize anything, don't improve anything along the way.

Before doing it, tell me exactly which file that text is in and on what line. After doing it, tell me one single sentence: whether this change shows up just by saving or whether I need to stop and restart the server.
tasks.expect: The new text shows up in the browser in under two seconds, with you not having reloaded anything. Look at the terminal and you'll see a new line like "compiled in 340ms."
tasks.stuck: If nothing changes, try in this order. One: press Ctrl+Shift+R (Cmd+Shift+R on Mac), which forces a reload ignoring anything the browser had cached. Two: check the terminal for red text, since then the change hasn't even been applied. Three: stop with Ctrl+C, start it again, and check. If after those three steps it's still the same, ask the AI: "Am I looking at the right file? Tell me which file is actually used to render this screen."

tasks.title: Break it on purpose to recognize blank A
tasks.where: In the terminal and the browser, at the same time
tasks.action: This is training, and it's worth doing even if it seems silly. Go to the terminal window, click inside it to select it, and press Ctrl+C. On Windows it might ask "Terminate batch job (Y/N)?": type Y and press Enter. You'll see the cursor come back and the terminal stop being busy. Now go to the browser and press F5 to reload. Read the message that shows up slowly and remember what it looks like. Then go back to the terminal and start it again with the same command as before. Trick: press the up arrow and the last command you typed shows up. Then reload the browser.
tasks.expect: Stopping the server, the browser tells you "This site can't be reached." Smaller, you'll see "localhost refused to connect" or ERR_CONNECTION_REFUSED. Starting it again and reloading, your website reappears. You just watched blank A be born and die under your control.
tasks.stuck: If Ctrl+C doesn't stop anything, make sure you clicked inside the terminal window before pressing it. If the focus is on the browser, Ctrl+C just copies text. If it's still running anyway, close the whole window with the X and open it again. If reloading the browser still shows your website with the server off, press Ctrl+Shift+R: you were looking at a previously cached copy.

tasks.title: Open the browser console and learn to copy the first error
tasks.where: In your browser, with the project open at localhost
tasks.action: With your website in front of you, press F12. A panel opens on the side or at the bottom. Above that panel there are tabs: find the one that says "Console" and click it. If the panel comes out very narrow, drag its edge to make it bigger. Now reload the page with F5 and watch what shows up. Find the very first red line, starting from the top, right-click on it, and choose "Copy message." If there's no red line at all, your project is clean: press F12 again to close it and move on.
tasks.expect: A panel with tabs and, in the console one, zero red lines (healthy project) or one or several red lines starting with words like "Uncaught," "Failed to load," or "TypeError." Ignore any yellow warnings: even your bank's website has those.
tasks.stuck: If F12 does nothing, try Ctrl+Shift+J on Windows or Cmd+Option+J on Mac. If you have a laptop whose function keys control volume and brightness, you might need Fn+F12. If the panel opens in a language you don't recognize or with odd tabs, don't hunt around: take a full screenshot and hand it to the AI asking "where's the console here?"

tasks.title: Diagnose a real blank screen with the three-source prompt
tasks.where: In the AI app, with the browser and terminal visible so you can copy from both
tasks.action: Save this prompt somewhere fixed, because you'll use it dozens of times. The key is that you bring the AI all three sources of information at once: what the browser says, what the terminal says, and what the console says. Most people bring just one and that's why they get answers made in the dark. Fill in the three blanks by literally copying and pasting, without summarizing or translating anything.
tasks.prompt:
My project isn't showing up in the browser and I need to know where the problem is before touching any code. I'm giving you three sources of information. Don't assume anything that isn't written here.

ADDRESS I OPENED: [paste the exact address here, with http:// and the port]

WHAT I SEE IN THE BROWSER: [describe which of these three it is: (A) a browser message saying it can't reach the site, (B) a completely blank, empty screen but with the title in the tab, (C) a screen with a big error message. Copy the text as-is if there is any]

WHAT THE TERMINAL SAYS: [paste the terminal's last 15 lines here, as-is, including the line saying what address it started on]

WHAT THE BROWSER CONSOLE SAYS (F12): [paste the entire first red error here, or write "no red errors"]

With that, answer me in this order, don't skip any point:
1. In one sentence: is the problem that the server isn't serving the page, or that the page arrives and breaks? Tell me what specific piece of data you're basing that on.
2. The most likely cause, just one.
3. Exactly what I do to fix it, as numbered steps, telling me at each step whether it's in the terminal, the browser, or a file.
4. How I know it worked: what I should see on screen.

If what I gave you doesn't let you decide between two causes, don't pick one at random: tell me exactly what piece of data you're missing and where I look for it.
tasks.expect: A diagnosis that starts by distinguishing whether the page arrived or not, then a cause, then steps. If it jumps straight to "let's rewrite the component" without answering point 1, it started from the roof.
tasks.stuck: If it suggests big code changes for a problem that smells like blank A, cut it off: "Before touching any file: the terminal says it started on port X and I was opening port Y. Is that it?" And if it gives you three possible causes at once, ask: "Rank them by probability and tell me how I rule out the first one in under thirty seconds."

tasks.title: Free up the port when it says it's taken
tasks.where: In the terminal, then in the AI app
tasks.action: If starting up gives you "Port 3000 is already in use" or "EADDRINUSE," an earlier program stayed running, often one of yours from yesterday you never stopped. You have two ways out. The easy one: accept the new port it offers (3001) and open that address, which works just as well. The clean one: kill the program occupying 3000, using the prompt below. Important warning before doing this: the command that shuts down a program by its identifier number is immediate and has no undo, so if you get the number wrong you could suddenly close something else you had open unsaved. Save whatever you have in progress before running it, and read carefully the program's name it shows you.
tasks.prompt:
When starting my project I get this error: [paste the full error here].

I'm on [Windows / Mac], I don't know how to code, and I'm going to copy and paste literally what you tell me.

Give me two separate commands, not one combined:

FIRST: the command that only LOOKS at what program is using that port, without closing anything. Explain to me which column in the result is the program's identifier number and how I know which program it is, so I can make sure I'm not about to close something important.

SECOND: the command that closes that specific program, with a blank marked XXXX where I have to put the number from the first one. Don't write it with a made-up number.

Then tell me: what's the sign, after running the second one, that the port is free again? And also tell me if there's any program name that, if it shows up in the first command, should make me stop and not close it.
tasks.expect: Two clear commands. On Windows the first will look something like netstat -ano | findstr :3000, which gives you back a row with a number at the end; on Mac it'll be something like lsof -ti:3000. Running the second with the correct number, the terminal says nothing, and starting your project again grabs 3000.
tasks.stuck: If it makes you nervous, don't do it: use the port it offers and keep working, you lose absolutely nothing. The alternative that always fixes it with no weird commands is restarting the computer, which shuts down every hung program at once. If the name shown occupying the port isn't node or python or anything you recognize as part of your project, don't close it and ask the AI what it is before touching it.

tasks.title: View it on your phone, on the same wifi
tasks.where: In the terminal first, then in your phone's browser
tasks.action: Localhost only works for your computer, but there's an intermediate trick before publishing anything: inside your home, devices on the same wifi can see each other. Many tools already give you that address at startup, on a line that says "Network:" followed by something like http://192.168.1.42:3000. If your terminal shows it, type that address into your phone's browser, with your phone connected to the same wifi as the computer. If that line doesn't show up, ask the AI how to start your project with local network access (in Vite you add --host, in Next.js you add -H 0.0.0.0). It's useful for what fails most at the start: seeing whether buttons overflow on a small screen.
tasks.expect: Your website on your phone, with the address starting with 192.168 or 10.0, not localhost. You'll see new lines show up in the terminal every time the phone requests the page.
tasks.stuck: If your phone loads nothing, check the obvious first: that it's on your home wifi and not on mobile data. If it still doesn't work, it's usually the Windows firewall, which the first time pops up a window asking permission, and you need to click "Allow access" on private networks. And if you're on an office, library, or coffee shop wifi, it's normal for it not to work: many public networks isolate devices on purpose. It's not your project's fault.

tasks.title: Write your startup cheat sheet and leave it inside the project
tasks.where: In the AI app, inside the project
tasks.action: What you just learned is going to fade in two weeks if you don't write it down, and it'll happen exactly when you're in the biggest hurry. Ask for a short file that lives inside the project folder, one anyone could follow without knowing anything, yourself included three months from now. Once it's made, open it and read it top to bottom once: if there's a step you don't understand, it's poorly written and you need to ask it to clarify.
tasks.prompt:
Create a file called HOW-TO-START.md in this project's root. It's aimed at a person who doesn't code and is opening this project after months of not touching it. No untranslated jargon and no assuming prior knowledge.

Exact structure, with these headings:

## Starting it
The steps numbered from scratch: opening the terminal, positioning in the folder (with the full path written out), the startup command, and the browser address. Include which terminal line confirms it went well.

## Stopping it
How to shut it down and why it needs to be done.

## If the screen is blank
A three-row table, one per symptom: (1) the browser says it can't reach the site, (2) a completely blank, empty screen, (3) a screen with an error message. In each row: what it means, where I look first, and what I do.

## Things that break this
The three or four most likely mistakes specific to THIS project, not in the abstract. For example, if there's an .env file without which it won't start, say so.

Style rules: each command on its own line, ready to copy and paste. Short sentences. No "simply" or "just." One page max.
tasks.expect: A HOW-TO-START.md file in the project folder, openable with a double-click, with your real folder path written inside and a three-row table for blank screens.
tasks.stuck: If the file comes out with generic steps like "navigate to your working directory," send it back: "Replace every vague instruction with this project's literal path and command. If you don't know a path, ask me instead of writing a made-up example." And if it comes out three pages long with theory, ask it to cut it in half, removing anything that's explanation and leaving only what to do.

matters: Reading the address in the terminal every time you start it, instead of typing it from memory. The port only changes when the usual one is taken and nobody warns you with a sign: it's told to you by a discreet line lost among ten others. Ignoring that line is what cost Nacho two days of asking the AI to fix flawless code.

Telling blank A apart from blank B before touching anything. They're two different worlds: one gets fixed in the terminal in ten seconds and the other in the code. Mix them up and you'll ask the AI to rewrite files that were perfectly fine, and every unnecessary rewrite introduces new bugs that weren't there before.

Checking the terminal before the browser. The terminal is the only one that sees the whole process, and when something fails while compiling it writes it there in red, with the file and line, while the browser just shows you the empty result. Diagnosing by looking at the browser is like investigating a fire by looking only at the smoke.

That the server has to be on, always, and that you're the one turning it on and off. It's the concept most people take for granted and fewest truly understand: your website doesn't exist if nobody's serving it. Understanding this is half of understanding what publishing it on the internet later means, where the only thing that changes is whose computer is turned on.
ignore: Everything about HTTPS, certificates, and the browser's padlock. On localhost there's no padlock and you don't need one: there's no stretch of network to eavesdrop on, since the request never even leaves your computer. This starts mattering the day you publish, and that day the platform you publish on handles it on its own.

Picking the port by hand and arguments about which number is better. It makes exactly zero difference whether it's 3000, 3001, or 4173, and there's no consequence to using one or another while working on your computer. Use whatever the tool gives you and move on.

Docker, Nginx, containers, and all the vocabulary that shows up when you search "local server" on Google. Those solve problems that start when a team of several people has to work on the same thing at once. You, with one project and one terminal, have plenty for many months.
canDo: Read a terminal or browser console error and translate it into a sentence you understand. It's what it does best out of all this: paste it a wall of English text and it tells you, in one line, what's missing.
Give you the exact command for your operating system, which is where most people get lost copying Mac tutorials while on Windows. Tell it which one you're on and it nails it practically every time.

Write you your specific project's startup cheat sheet, with your real paths and commands, instead of a generic manual. It also knows how to give you the command that frees an occupied port on your system.
Fix the code errors causing a true blank screen, if you paste the entire first red error. Many are a single line and it solves them in one message.
cantDo: See your screen. It doesn't know whether the server's running, what port it started on, or what's showing in your browser, unless you copy and paste it to it. When it answers without that data, it's guessing politely.

Start or stop the server for you from the chat app. That Enter is yours to press. There are tools that do run things on your computer, but typing in ChatGPT's, Claude's, or Gemini's text box isn't one of them.

Know why your browser shows you an old version of the page. That cached copy is inside your browser and the AI can't see it; the forced reload with Ctrl+Shift+R is yours to do, and it's worth trying before assuming something's broken.

Guess problems with your network or computer: a firewall blocking it, an antivirus getting jumpy about the port, an office wifi that isolates devices. It can suggest where to look, but you're the one who checks.
words: A word that means "this computer, the one in front of me." When you type it into the browser, the page is served by your own machine and the request never goes outside.
The number that means the same thing as localhost. It's reserved worldwide to point to oneself, so on your computer it points to your computer and on your neighbor's, to theirs.
The number after the colon, like 3000. It's for telling which of the running programs you're asking, the same way an apartment number tells who you're calling inside a building.
A computer, or a program inside a computer, whose job is to wait for someone to request a page and hand it over. While you're learning, that's you.

The program that runs while you're building, so you can see your project and have it update on its own every time you change something. It turns off when you're done and has nothing to do with what people will see once you publish.
The window where you type commands with the keyboard instead of clicking buttons. It's intimidating because it has no graphics, but it only does exactly what you type, no more, no less.
The two keys pressed together inside the command window to shut down whatever's running there. Outside that window, those same keys copy text, so you need to click inside it first.
The browser page updating on its own as soon as you save a change, with no reload from you. It's what makes working fast instead of a constant back-and-forth.
A hidden screen that opens with F12 where the page logs everything happening to it, failures included. You don't need to understand what it says: you need to copy and paste it.
A copy of the page the browser saves to show it to you faster next time. Sometimes it shows you the old copy even after you've changed things, which is why the forced reload with Ctrl+Shift+R exists.
